# II. The Controller Cases

Delaware cleanses a controller's deal only when the protections bind the controller before it bargains; a protection the controller can threaten its way past, or one it adds after the price is set, leaves the burden on the defendants. Three decisions mark that line.

In Kahn v. Lynch Communication Systems, the controller threatened a hostile tender offer if the special committee did not accept its price.[^1] The threat meant the committee could not say no, so its approval shifted nothing.

In Kahn v. M & F Worldwide Corp., by contrast, the controller conditioned its offer from the outset on approval by an independent committee and a majority of the minority.[^2] Because both conditions bound the controller before negotiations began, business-judgment review applied. Read together with Lynch, the case shows that timing and the power to refuse, not the mere presence of a committee, do the cleansing work.

[^1]: Kahn v. Lynch Commc'n Sys., Inc., 638 A.2d 1110, 1117 (Del. 1994).
[^2]: Kahn v. M & F Worldwide Corp., 88 A.3d 635, 644 (Del. 2014).
